title: A Preregistered Audit of Dataset Contamination Controls in LLM-for-NetOps Benchmarks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, confirmatory audit to evaluate conservative deterministic contamination detectors (exact normalized token equality; fuzzy 5‑gram overlap; provenance heuristics) and a guarded exclusion policy on a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample. Execution artifacts show the run sampled provenance‑stable synthetic tasks and used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one generation reused for baseline+guarded), which made the primary paired estimand (guarded − baseline success rate) untestable in this execution. No preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags occurred and both baseline and guarded validator pass rates were 150/150. Paired success‑rate difference = 0.0 percentage points (95% bootstrap CI [0.0,0.0]); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. We document the preregistration→execution mismatch with concrete artifact citations (preregistration SHA‑256: 9a5e11c5b2b1c14c2a4a874a7ad0b9f215f8477a7becf4eb6dd1c0ff6a00ae7a; execution artifacts: execution/task_manifest.jsonl sha256=b7c08599e3f96d8d5605a18f8f973e0707d7224327eeed7bde78c0d34cb83e55; execution/model_configuration.json sha256=a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820), explain why the run was degenerate for detecting web‑sourced contamination, and give artifact‑anchored recommendations (provenance‑rich sampling, independent per‑condition generation, full per‑item overlap persistence, multi‑model replication, paraphrase‑robust detectors) to make future audits sensitive to contamination.

sections.introduction:
Motivation. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation and automated configuration repair. Operational decisions based on benchmark results require that measured performance reflect model capability rather than dataset contamination (e.g., benchmark items present in model training corpora) or construct invalidity (templated low‑complexity items). Surveys and recent benchmark work therefore recommend contamination detectors, provenance tracing, and validator‑backed oracles.

Research question and contribution. We preregistered a confirmatory audit to answer: under conservative deterministic contamination detectors (exact normalized equality; fuzzy 5‑gram overlap with preregistered thresholds; provenance timestamp heuristics) and a guarded exclusion policy, how many high‑confidence flags arise in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample, and how much does applying those controls change a single hosted LLM’s validator pass rate? The run produced artifact‑verified quantities and a clear preregistration→execution mismatch that renders the primary paired test uninformative for generation‑level contamination in this execution. Our contributions are: (1) a fully preregistered confirmatory execution archived (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1; preregistration SHA‑256 = 9a5e11c5b2b1c14c2a4a874a7ad0b9f215f8477a7becf4eb6dd1c0ff6a00ae7a); (2) exact, artifact‑verified confirmatory statistics on Npairs = 150 with deterministic validator traces; and (3) an explicit preregistration→execution reconciliation (table below) that cites execution artifacts and identifies why the outcome is degenerate, plus concrete artifact‑anchored recommendations to increase audit sensitivity.

Scope and bounded claims. The execution sampled provenance‑stable synthetic tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; generation semantics reused a single model response per item for both baseline and guarded episodes (shared_initial_candidate). These two artifact‑verified facts limit inference: the observed zero‑flag, zero‑difference outcome applies only to this deterministic synthetic sampling and shared‑generation regime and does not imply absence of contamination in independent public benchmarks.
sections.related_work:
LLM-driven NetOps and validators. Prior work shows LLMs can synthesize device configs or repairs; integrating deterministic verifiers or validate–repair loops improves average repair quality compared to naive generation. Formal verification and network analysis tools (header‑space style analyzers, localized subspecification) can act as practical oracles for reachability and policy correctness.

Evaluation‑validity critiques. Surveys and meta‑analyses highlight contamination (benchmark items present in model training data) and construct invalidity (templated items) as recurring risks. Proposed defenses include deterministic fingerprinting, fuzzy n‑gram overlap, provenance tracing, and human adjudication. Our study implements a conservative subset of these defenses in a preregistered confirmatory design and focuses on an artifact‑grounded reconciliation when the execution choices limited audit sensitivity.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand. The experiment was preregistered as contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1 (preregistration SHA‑256 = 9a5e11c5b2b1c14c2a4a874a7ad0b9f215f8477a7becf4eb6dd1c0ff6a00ae7a). The primary estimand was the paired success‑rate difference: guarded − baseline across item×model pairs, analyzed by paired_binary_analysis_v1 using an exact McNemar two‑sided test. The preregistration listed four public OpenAlex benchmarks as the intended benchmark_scope (see preregistration evidence_record_ids) but allowed deterministic synthetic generation when reproducibility and artifact stability were required.

Sampling, generation semantics, and deterministic implementation. The executed sample of 150 items was produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and is recorded in execution/task_manifest.jsonl (artifact: execution/task_manifest.jsonl; sha256=b7c08599e3f96d8d5605a18f8f973e0707d7224327eeed7bde78c0d34cb83e55). The model configuration used in execution is archived at execution/model_configuration.json (artifact: execution/model_configuration.json; sha256=a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820) and declares declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" and independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate semantics). Because independent_condition_generation was false, the pipeline made a single hosted model generation per item and reused that shared candidate for both baseline and guarded episodes unless an exclusion/replacement was triggered; provider accounting shows model_calls_used = 150 while planned maximum_model_calls = 300 (execution manifest fields archived in the bundle).

Contamination detectors, thresholds, and persistence policy. The preregistered detector suite implemented: (1) exact normalized token equality, (2) fuzzy 5‑gram shingle overlap with preregistered high‑confidence threshold ≥0.80 (and lower thresholds for sensitivity), and (3) provenance timestamp heuristics comparing item metadata to model cutoff dates. The preregistration specified that the detector workflow persist detailed per‑item fuzzy overlap tables only when threshold crossings or replacements occurred to limit artifact size. This persistence policy is recorded in the transformation manifest (artifact path: execution/transformation_manifest.json; full manifest of artifact hashes documented under execution/execution_manifest.json in the archive). The analysis artifact that records flagged items is analysis/contamination_summary.csv (artifact: analysis/contamination_summary.csv; sha256=389227f0d1e81239c7498abd4944a04c59c92c5fa042b990e332796cd61c3222).

Guarded policy and replacements. The preregistered guarded policy excluded deterministic high‑confidence flags (exact match OR 5‑gram overlap ≥0.80) and deterministically replaced excluded items via deterministic retemplating with fixed seeds; replacements required intent similarity (preregistered embedding cosine ≥0.85). Replacement traces and rule artifacts would be archived when replacements occur. In this execution no high‑confidence flags or replacements were performed (analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty, sha256 above).

Validator and scoring. The deterministic oracle was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0). For each candidate it parsed commands, updated an explicit device state model, and checked required_final_state and workflow constraints. The validator emitted a binary pass/fail and detailed trace fields for each episode; these traces are archived per episode and underpin the binary outcomes used for analysis (see execution/scoring/*.json and execution/raw_results.jsonl; artifact execution/raw_results.jsonl sha256=5337998d1d86aca507f77659d75cc9487cf3d87a157ed5044b8a9d5ff79b5586).

Analysis plan and preregistered sensitivity checks. Primary analysis used exact McNemar two‑sided test and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Prespecified sensitivity analyses included treating failed calls as failures and fuzzy‑threshold sensitivity (0.50, 0.65, 0.80). All code, seeds, and analysis artifacts are archived; paired contingency output is analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (artifact sha256=c2ba9cdb5d0938eae910129ba511eadf309319e6e05b36d9e3b4860032deb80e).

Preregistration→execution reconciliation (compact). Table 1 below maps key preregistered values to executed values with concrete artifact citations and SHA‑256 hashes where available.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary outcomes. Execution completed planned_episode_count = 300 (150 item pairs) with completed_episode_count = 300 and failed_episode_count = 0. Because independent_condition_generation = false and no high‑confidence exclusions occurred, provider call accounting shows model_calls_used = 150 (one shared generation per item) rather than two independent generations per item; this is recorded in the execution manifest and in execution/model_configuration.json (sha256=a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820).

Contamination detectors and absence of high‑confidence flags. The preregistered detectors produced zero high‑confidence flags for the executed sample; analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty (artifact sha256=389227f0d1e81239c7498abd4944a04c59c92c5fa042b990e332796cd61c3222). Because of the detector persistence policy (detailed in execution/transformation_manifest.json; full artifact manifests are available in execution/execution_manifest.json), the pipeline persisted detailed per‑item fuzzy overlap outputs only when a threshold crossing or replacement occurred; no such records exist for this run.

Validator outcomes and confirmatory statistics. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 returned pass for all baseline episodes (baseline_success_count = 150/150; baseline_success_rate = 1.0) and for all guarded episodes (guarded_success_count = 150/150; guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 150, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; sha256=c2ba9cdb5d0938eae910129ba511eadf309319e6e05b36d9e3b4860032deb80e). The paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0 percentage points; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. These numbers are direct reads of archived analysis artifacts.

Representative diagnostic. Representative episode traces (e.g., pair‑000001 in execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json and execution/responses/task-000001-*.txt) show identical shared_initial_candidate, baseline, and guarded responses and full validator traces indicating parsed_command_count, required_command_count, normalized_configuration, and valid=true. Example response artifact: execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt (sha256=8f38c8becd7e1e36d8902e9ba2f09218baad021d77365b20eb52914a4bdf4080) and its scoring JSON are archived.
sections.discussion:
Why the primary estimand was untestable in this execution. Two artifact‑verified execution facts explain the degenerate concordance (n11=150): (1) the confirmatory sample consisted of provenance‑stable synthetic items (execution/task_manifest.jsonl; sha256=b7c08599e3f96d8d5605a18f8f973e0707d7224327eeed7bde78c0d34cb83e55) and (2) the pipeline used shared_initial_candidate semantics (execution/model_configuration.json; sha256=a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820), which reused a single model generation per item for baseline and guarded episodes when no exclusions occurred. Under those conditions the paired test cannot observe generation‑level discordance unless exclusions trigger replacements.

Absence of a global per‑item overlap table and its consequence. The detector persistence policy (execution/transformation_manifest.json; full file listing in execution/execution_manifest.json) archived only threshold‑crossing records. Because no high‑confidence crossings occurred, no global per‑item fuzzy overlap table was produced; analysis/contamination_summary.csv (sha256=389227f0...) is empty. This artifact‑grounded absence means the archive does not include the per‑item fuzzy‑overlap distribution that would allow post‑hoc assessment of how close items were to the 0.80 threshold. To remedy this gap future audits should persist per‑item overlap scores unconditionally.

Design changes to increase audit sensitivity (artifact‑anchored recommendations). The archived run supports the following concrete changes to make a paired contamination audit informative for web‑sourced benchmarks: (1) sample public items with explicit provenance metadata (URLs/DOIs and timestamps) so provenance heuristics are meaningful (preregistration originally listed four OpenAlex IDs as benchmark_scope); (2) set independent_condition_generation = true to force independent baseline vs guarded generations and thereby raise the probability of discordant pairs; (3) persist full per‑item fuzzy overlap scores (new artifact e.g., analysis/contamination_scores.csv) regardless of threshold crossing; (4) expand to multi‑model replication and multiple seeds to increase power; and (5) add paraphrase‑sensitive detectors plus human adjudication for borderline cases. Each recommendation follows directly from explicit gaps visible in archived artifacts (model_calls_used = 150 vs planned_maximum_model_calls = 300; empty analysis/contamination_summary.csv; absence of per‑item overlap table).

Operational implications. The artifact‑verified validator traces confirm that deterministic_netops_validator_v5 can assert functional correctness for the executed synthetic tasks. However, auditors should not extrapolate the present degenerate null to public benchmarks: this execution does not test web‑sourced contamination or paraphrase leakage. Practical operational audits should therefore combine provenance‑rich sampling, independent generations, multi‑model checks, and human adjudication.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired audit. In the reproducible 150‑pair synthetic sample we observed zero preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags and identical validator pass rates (150/150 baseline, 150/150 guarded). Artifact evidence (execution/task_manifest.jsonl sha256=b7c08599e3f96d8d5605a18f8f973e0707d7224327eeed7bde78c0d34cb83e55; execution/model_configuration.json sha256=a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820; preregistration SHA‑256 = 9a5e11c5b2b1c14c2a4a874a7ad0b9f215f8477a7becf4eb6dd1c0ff6a00ae7a) shows the paired test was rendered uninformative by provenance‑stable synthetic sampling and shared generation semantics. We therefore (a) reclassify the primary confirmatory estimand as untestable/degenerate in this execution and (b) provide artifact‑anchored recommendations (provenance‑rich sampling, independent per‑condition generation, unconditional per‑item overlap persistence, multi‑model replication, paraphrase‑robust detectors) to make future preregistered audits sensitive to real‑world contamination. All raw responses, validator traces, execution manifests, and analysis artifacts cited above are archived in the execution bundle and are available for inspection. The primary numeric results reported here are direct reads of archived analysis artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv sha256=c2ba9cdb5d0938eae910129ba511eadf309319e6e05b36d9e3b4860032deb80e; analysis/contamination_summary.csv sha256=389227f0d1e81239c7498abd4944a04c59c92c5fa042b990e332796cd61c3222).

limitations: Single‑model execution (gpt‑5-mini) — results do not generalize across other LLM families, sizes, or training corpora.

Sampled items were provenance‑stable synthetic/deterministically generated tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") for this run; absence of high‑confidence flags here may not reflect contamination prevalence in real‑world, web‑crawled benchmarks.

Generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate across baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical model outputs when no exclusions occurred and thus limiting sensitivity to interventions that rely on independent re‑generation.

Contamination detection relied on preregistered conservative heuristics (exact match and fuzzy 5‑gram overlap thresholds); subtler contamination patterns (paraphrased memorization, partial leakage) may escape these heuristics and require richer provenance or human adjudication.

Passing the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 indicates satisfaction of the checked functional constraints but does not imply comprehensive production readiness or absence of semantic regressions outside the validator's scope.
